explains Kruskal handling: Kruskal naturally produces a Minimum Spanning Forest without modification; processes all edges and stops when no more edges can connect disjoint sets (yielding V - C edges where C is component count)

explains Prim handling: standard Prim stops after completing the MST of the initial starting component; must be wrapped in an outer loop over all unvisited vertices to restart Prim on remaining components
highlights edge count: total edges in forest is always `V - C`

questions.question: How does the Dinic's Algorithm for Maximum Network Flow improve upon Edmonds-Karp by using Level Graphs and Blocking Flows to achieve O(V^2 * E) time?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Level Graph: BFS from source assigns exact hop distance `level[u]` to each node; edges only point forward where `level[v] == level[u] + 1`
defines Blocking Flow: a flow in the level graph such that every path from s to t contains at least one saturated edge
traces algorithm phase: 1. Construct Level Graph via BFS in O(E); 2. Push Blocking Flow via DFS in O(V * E); repeat until sink is unreachable in BFS
proves complexity: level of sink strictly increases in each phase (at most V phases); total runtime is O(V * (V * E)) = O(V^2 * E) (and O(E * sqrt(V)) on unit networks)

questions.question: What is the difference between Kahn's Algorithm and Tarjan's SCC Algorithm in identifying deadlocked threads waiting on mutual exclusion locks?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Wait-For Graph (WFG): directed graph where vertices represent threads and directed edges u -> v represent thread u waiting for a lock held by thread v

evaluates Kahn's algorithm: topologically sorts WFG; threads with in-degree > 0 after queue depletion identify the set of deadlocked threads, but cannot easily separate independent isolated deadlock cycles
evaluates Tarjan's algorithm: partitions WFG into Strongly Connected Components; any SCC with more than 1 vertex (or self-loop) represents an isolated, independent deadlock cycle
highlights Tarjan's diagnosis advantage: isolates distinct deadlock cycles, allowing the runtime to terminate or abort a single thread from each cycle to resolve contention

questions.question: How does the Sliding Window Maximum problem run in O(N) time using a Monotonic Double-Ended Queue (Deque) instead of an O(N log K) priority queue?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: identifies priority queue flaw: standard heap does not support efficient deletion of elements sliding out of the window, requiring lazy deletion taking O(N log K) time
defines Monotonic Deque: stores indices; elements corresponding to indices are strictly maintained in descending order (maximum element index always at front)

traces iteration for element X at index i: 1. Pop back while deque not empty and `arr[deque.back()] <= X` (elements smaller than X can never be the maximum); 2. Push index i to back; 3. Pop front if `deque.front() <= i - K` (expired from window)
proves O(N) complexity: each array index is pushed once and popped once from the deque, running in strictly linear O(N) time

questions.question: What is an Escape Analysis optimization in the JVM, and how does Scalar Replacement eliminate heap allocation by allocating object fields directly to CPU registers and stack frames?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Escape Analysis: JIT compiler analyzes object scope; determines whether an object reference escapes the executing method or thread (e.g. passed to outside methods, returned, or assigned to fields)
defines NoEscape: object is created, used, and discarded entirely within a single method without escaping

explains Scalar Replacement: JIT compiler breaks the object into its individual primitive fields (scalars) and allocates them directly into CPU registers or stack frames rather than allocating heap memory
highlights GC benefit: completely eliminates heap allocation and garbage collection overhead for short-lived temporary objects (like Builders, Iterators, and Points)

questions.question: How does Biased Locking in HotSpot JVM optimize uncontended synchronized blocks, and why was Biased Locking deprecated and disabled in modern Java 15+?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Biased Locking: assumes most monitors are acquired repeatedly by the same thread; writes the thread ID directly into the object's Mark Word once via CAS; subsequent locks by the same thread require zero atomic instructions
identifies revocation penalty: when a different thread contends for a biased object, the bias must be revoked; revoking bias requires bringing ALL threads to a global STOP-THE-WORLD SAFEPOINT

explains why modern runtimes deprecated it (JEP 374): modern reactive and thread-pool architectures frequently pass objects across threads; the massive STW pause latency from thousands of lock revocations far outweighed the savings of uncontended CAS atomic instructions
notes replacement: modern JVMs default directly to lightweight stack-based CAS locking without bias

questions.question: What is the False Sharing problem in multi-threaded concurrent data structures, and how does the @Contended annotation in Java 8+ enforce cache line padding?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines False Sharing: two threads on different CPU cores write to independent variables that happen to share the same 64-byte CPU cache line

explains hardware bus thrashing: Core 1's write invalidates the cache line in Core 2's L1 cache via the MESI coherence protocol, forcing constant re-fetching over the memory bus even though threads access different variables
explains historical padding: developers manually declared 7-8 unused dummy `long` fields (56-64 bytes) to push variables onto separate cache lines

explains `@jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended`: instructs the JVM compiler and classloader to automatically isolate the annotated field or class with 128 bytes of padding, eliminating false sharing cleanly

questions.question: How does the Trie with Failure Links implement the Aho-Corasick BFS construction step to build suffix transitions in O(Sigma * Alphabet) time?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: initializes BFS queue: root's direct children have their failure links set directly to root and are enqueued
traces BFS node processing: for current node u with failure link `fail[u]`, inspect each child node v with character c
updates failure link: find `fail[u]`'s child on character c; if absent, follow failure links upstream until finding matching transition or root; set `fail[v]` to that target node
merges output lists: `output[v] = output[v] U output[fail[v]]`, ensuring that finding an occurrence of a longer word automatically flags occurrences of its shorter embedded suffix words

questions.question: What is a Treap Persistent Data Structure, and how does Path Copying create functional immutable data structures that preserve version history in O(log N) space per update?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Fully Persistent Data Structure: all versions of the data structure persist and remain queryable and modifiable over time; updating version V1 produces version V2 without destroying V1
identifies naive flaw: copying the entire tree on each write consumes O(N) memory per version

explains Path Copying: duplicate ONLY the nodes along the direct path from root down to the modified leaf (at most O(log N) nodes); all unmodified subtrees are shared by pointing directly to existing nodes from previous versions
calculates efficiency: update creates O(log N) new nodes and runs in O(log N) time, achieving full historical versioning with minimal memory overhead

questions.question: What is the difference between QuickSelect and IntroSelect in order-statistic finding, and how does IntroSelect guarantee worst-case O(N) time?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: explains QuickSelect: partitioning algorithm similar to QuickSort; recurses into only ONE partition containing the target rank K; achieves average O(N) time
identifies QuickSelect worst-case: pathological pivot selections (e.g. sorted input) degrade to O(N^2) time
explains IntroSelect (Introspective Selection): monitors recursion depth cutoff (`2 * log N`); if partitions remain unbalanced, falls back to the deterministic Median-of-Medians algorithm
guarantees worst-case bound: combines the fast practical speed of QuickSelect with the guaranteed O(N) worst-case bound of Median-of-Medians, used in C++ `std::nth_element`

questions.question: How does Kasai's Algorithm compute the Longest Common Prefix (LCP) array from a Suffix Array in strictly linear O(N) time?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: identifies naive LCP flaw: comparing adjacent suffixes in the suffix array character-by-character takes O(N^2) worst-case time
states Kasai's key observation: if suffix starting at index `i` has LCP `h` with its predecessor in the suffix array, then suffix starting at `i + 1` has LCP of AT LEAST `h - 1` with its predecessor
traces algorithm: iterate in original text order (`i = 0 to N-1`); locate suffix `i` in suffix array using rank array; start checking LCP from `h = max(0, h - 1)` instead of starting from zero
proves O(N) time: the prefix comparison counter `h` increases at most N times and decrements at most N times, running in strictly linear O(N) time

questions.question: What is the difference between Kruskal's Algorithm and the Boruvka Algorithm for Minimum Spanning Trees, and why is Boruvka naturally suited for parallel distributed computing (e.g. MapReduce)?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Boruvka's algorithm: in each round, every connected component concurrently finds its cheapest outgoing edge; all selected edges are added to the MST and components are merged
proves O(log V) rounds: each round contracts the number of components by at least half (at most `V / 2` components remain), guaranteeing termination in at most `log2(V)` rounds

contrasts with Kruskal: Kruskal is strictly sequential (must process edges one-by-one in sorted order across the global graph); Boruvka executes edge selections independently across components in parallel
highlights distributed computing: Boruvka is the foundational MST algorithm for distributed graph frameworks (Pregel, Apache Spark GraphX)

questions.question: How does the Segment Tree with Lazy Propagation solve the Range Assignment and Range Sum problem without state inconsistency?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines operations: `set(L, R, val)` (sets all elements in range to val) and `sum(L, R)` (returns sum of elements in range)
explains Segment Tree node state: stores `sum` and an `assigned_val` lazy tag (with boolean `has_lazy`)
explains lazy update rule: when setting range to `val`, update `sum = val * (segment_length)`; set `assigned_val = val`, completely overwriting any prior lazy additions or assignments
explains `pushDown()` to children: pushes `assigned_val` to both left and right children, updating their sums and setting their lazy tags before recursing downward

questions.question: What is the difference between Thread Pools using Work-Stealing (ForkJoinPool) versus Work-Sharing (ThreadPoolExecutor) in handling recursive task decomposition?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: defines Work-Sharing (`ThreadPoolExecutor`): all worker threads compete for tasks from a SINGLE shared blocking queue (`BlockingQueue`); under high concurrency, lock contention on the centralized queue becomes a severe bottleneck
defines Work-Stealing (`ForkJoinPool`): each worker thread maintains its OWN private Double-Ended Queue (Deque) of tasks; threads push and pop tasks from their own queue head without lock contention
explains Work Stealing: when an idle worker exhausts its own deque, it 'steals' tasks from the TAIL of another busy thread's deque using lock-free CAS
highlights recursive decomposition: ideal for divide-and-conquer parallel algorithms (e.g. parallel streams, parallel sorting) where tasks spawn smaller sub-tasks

questions.question: In enterprise low-latency Java architecture, how does Off-Heap Memory allocation (using sun.misc.Unsafe or ByteBuffer.allocateDirect) eliminate Garbage Collection pauses entirely for high-throughput cache data?
questions.subject: OOP
criteria: identifies on-heap limitation: storing millions of cache entries on the Java heap creates massive GC root traversal overhead, triggering periodic Stop-The-World latency spikes of seconds or minutes
explains Off-Heap Allocation: allocates native memory outside the JVM garbage-collected heap using `ByteBuffer.allocateDirect()` or `Unsafe.allocateMemory()`
explains GC immunity: the JVM garbage collector never scans, traces, or moves off-heap memory blocks, completely eliminating GC pause times regardless of cache size (even for hundreds of gigabytes)

identifies operational trade-offs: requires manual memory deallocation (risk of native memory leaks), serialization/deserialization overhead to access fields, and risk of segmentation faults upon invalid pointer access
